title: The Holy King Who Forgives and Sends
introduction:
Before You Begin
 These commentaries grow out of this week’s passage. They are not required, and they are not the main thing. They are simply here to help, a little extra for your study. Feel free to use them or not, and to choose the point that best fits your group’s conversation. You do not need to cover everything. What matters most is to read the passage, pray, study it together and let it reach your hearts, so that we respond to God in obedience to his Word. Each point also opens other themes you can explore, as your time and energy allow. Our prayer is that God will guide you, give you wisdom and bring fruit from your time in his Word.

Only the Bible is inspired by God. These commentaries are human reflections, always read them under the authority of God’s Word.

“In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1). An earthly king had died, but the true King was still on his throne. In this chapter Isaiah sees God’s glory, discovers his own need, receives forgiveness and is sent with a very hard message. These four reflections follow the passage: the holiness of God, the prophet who falls under his own preaching, a readiness to serve that comes from love, and a message that many will not receive.
finalWord:
Optional Ideas to Explore
- Luke 13:4 to 5 · Not worse than others. About eighteen people killed when a tower fell, Jesus asked, “do you think that they were worse offenders than all the men who dwell in Jerusalem? I tell you, no.” Disasters are a call for all of us to turn to God, not a reason to judge the victims.
- Luke 8:10 · Seeing but not seeing. Jesus used Isaiah’s words to explain why he taught in parables. The same message that opens the eyes of some can leave others unmoved. The difference lies in the heart that hears.

points.title: The Holiness of God
points.text:
Around God’s throne stand the seraphim. “Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew” (Isaiah 6:2). Notice something important. They do not cover their faces because they are confessing sin. They are holy creatures. They cover their faces simply because they are creatures standing before the majesty of their Creator. Reverence does not always come from guilt. It comes from seeing who God is.

Theologians speak of God’s aseity. It means that God exists from himself and depends on nothing and no one. Everything else in the universe receives its life from him. He alone receives it from no one. That is why his glory is unique, and why worship belongs to him alone. No creature, however high, can share that place.

Then look at how the seraphim worship. The text does not only say that they sang to God. “One called to another, and said, ‘Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!’” (Isaiah 6:3). They proclaimed God’s holiness to each other. Worship is not only something we say to God. It also tells the people next to us who God is. When we sing together on Sunday, we are reminding one another of the truth. Paul says the same: “teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16).

Reflection question
 The seraphim covered their faces not because of guilt, but because of God’s greatness. How can seeing God’s holiness more clearly change the way we worship together, and the way we remind one another of who he is?

Optional Ideas to Explore
- Revelation 4:8 · The song that never stops. John also saw living creatures with six wings, who “have no rest day and night, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!’” Isaiah’s vision and John’s vision meet around the same throne.
- John 12:41 · Whose glory did Isaiah see? After quoting Isaiah, John writes, “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him.” John is speaking about Jesus. The holy King on the throne is the same Lord who came to us in Christ.

points.title: The Prophet Under His Own Preaching
points.text:
In chapter 5, Isaiah pronounced six “woes” against the sins of the people: “Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20), and many more. Then, in chapter 6, he sees God, and the next woe is for himself: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). The preacher ends up under his own preaching. A preacher who speaks against everyone’s sin but never sees his own has not yet understood the holiness of God.

Some theologians believe Isaiah was already serving as a prophet before this moment, and that here he receives a special and very serious calling. If so, his confession does not mean he had no faith before. A person can truly serve God for years and then, before a greater sight of his glory, discover how much they still need to be cleansed. This is precious for anyone who has served for a long time. Finding a weakness does not cancel all our past service. It may show us that a new task needs more humility, more clarity or more courage.

What were Isaiah’s “unclean lips”? Some theologians suggest they may also include words that were never spoken. Perhaps he had seen the sins of the people and their leaders, but had not spoken up as clearly as he should. Our lips can sin in three ways: when we say what we should not say, when we stay silent when we should speak, and when we say the right thing in the wrong way.

But God does not leave Isaiah in his guilt. A seraph touches his mouth with a burning coal from the altar: “your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven” (Isaiah 6:7). For a long time servant, this may not be the first time he is forgiven. It may be a deeper and clearer assurance of the grace he had already received.

Reflection question
 God did not crush Isaiah when he confessed his unclean lips. He cleansed him and then sent him. How can God’s forgiveness give us the courage to look honestly at our own words, both what we say and what we leave unsaid?

Optional Ideas to Explore
- Matthew 7:3 to 5 · First our own eye. Jesus asked, “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” Seeing our own sin first does not stop us from helping others. It is what makes us able to help them well.
- 1 Corinthians 9:27 · The preacher also needs grace. Paul writes that he disciplines himself “lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.” Even an apostle knew that the message he preached was also for him.

points.title: Grace That Moves Us to Serve
points.text:
After he is forgiven, Isaiah hears a question: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And he answers, “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). Notice the order. First grace, then calling. Isaiah does not volunteer to earn God’s favor. He volunteers because he has received it.

Some theologians see in Isaiah’s quick answer the fruit of a love that the Spirit had set on fire. Grace does not leave a person sitting still. When we see a need, and we know God has given us something to help with, we want to use it. This helps us tell the difference between a real desire to serve and a desire for a position. One looks at the need of others and the glory of God. The other looks at itself.

The task was not easy. God told Isaiah that many would not listen. His calling required faithfulness and endurance, precisely because it did not promise a warm welcome. But a hard message does not give anyone the right to become a hard person. Right after hearing it, Isaiah asks, “Lord, how long?” (Isaiah 6:11). He still cares about the people who will receive the warning.

Paul says that without love, even the greatest gifts are empty: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). Christian service that is ready, responsible before God and full of compassion grows out of love, not out of the wish to be seen.

Reflection question
 Isaiah said “Send me!” because he had first been forgiven. How can the grace we have received move us to serve others with love and compassion, even when the task is hard?

Optional Ideas to Explore
- 2 Corinthians 5:14 · The love that moves us. “For the love of Christ compels us.” Paul’s tireless service did not come from pressure or ambition, but from being loved by Christ.
- Luke 19:41 to 42 · Tears over the city. As Jesus came near Jerusalem, “he saw the city and wept over it.” The One who announced judgment also wept for the people who would suffer it. A true messenger of God carries both truth and tears.

points.title: A Message Many Will Not Receive
points.text:
Isaiah’s message is one of the hardest in the Bible. “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand. You see indeed, but don’t perceive’” (Isaiah 6:9). The New Testament quotes these words several times. Some passages show the responsibility of the people, who closed their own eyes. Others show God’s judgment. And others focus on the prophet’s mission. Theologians have noted that these views can stand together. God is sovereign, and at the same time, the guilt comes from the human heart that refuses him.

Luke ends the book of Acts with these words. Paul quotes Isaiah to the leaders in Rome who would not believe, and then adds, “the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen” (Acts 28:28). Even when some reject the message, God’s plan keeps moving forward.

There is also a strong contrast in this chapter. In verse 3, “The whole earth is full of his glory!” But by verses 11 and 12, the land is “utterly waste” and “the forsaken places are many.” A land full of glory can become a desolate land. Yet God’s glory and his rule do not disappear when judgment comes. And just as God once showed his presence in a burning bush in the desert, he can be present even in places that look empty. The chapter ends with a small sign of hope: “the holy seed is its stump” (Isaiah 6:13).

We must be careful here. This passage does not give us the right to say that every tragedy today is a specific punishment from God. Jesus himself warned against that kind of thinking (Luke 13:4 to 5).

Reflection question
 Isaiah was sent to people who often would not listen, yet God’s plan did not fail. How can trusting God’s sovereignty help us keep sharing his truth with patience and love, even when we see little response?
